patent: Filed 1951-05-11 and issued 1956-02-28 to Jay W. Forrester, assigned to Research Corporation. Forrester led Project Whirlwind at MIT; this is his patent on coincident-current magnetic core memory. Cores with a nearly rectangular hysteresis loop sit at the crossings of coordinate wires: a current giving H_{1} on one wire leaves a core unchanged, while H_{1} on two wires through the same core (2H_{1}) reverses it, so one of many cores is selected by energizing one wire per coordinate. Reading is destructive: the core is driven to the 0 state and a sense winding picks up a pulse only if it was holding a 1. Figs. 1-2 give the two-coordinate scheme and Figs. 3-4a extend it to three coordinates; the preferred three-coordinate method drives two coordinates and cancels the unwanted selections with an opposing current on the third, the role of the inhibit winding in later core memories. Figs. 5-9 carry the same selection over to ferroelectric capacitors. With n coordinates of A leads each, C = A^{n} cores are reached with nA leads (96 leads for 32768 cores in a cube of 32 on a side). Forrester published the three-dimensional scheme as "Digital Information Storage in Three Dimensions Using Magnetic Cores" (Journal of Applied Physics, 1951). A core memory was installed in Whirlwind in 1953. Ownership of core memory was contested; in 1964, after years of legal dispute, IBM paid MIT $13 million for rights to this patent. Coincident-current core memory coincident-current core memory was the main form of computer main memory until semiconductor memory replaced it in the 1970s.

figs.1: B-H loop. A and D are the two remanent states at zero applied field (1 and 0). Positive side, two-coordinate case: from D a single drive H_{1} only runs around the small loop L and falls back to D, while 2H_{1}, past the coercive force H_{c}, switches the core to A. Negative side, three-coordinate case: each drive gives H_{m}/3, so two together (2H_{m}/3) stay inside -H_{c} and all three (H_{m}) switch. The thin vertical lines run from each tick mark to the loop.
figs.2: Four toroidal cores C_{11}-C_{22}, each with three windings: y-coordinate coil 10 on the left, sensing coil 12 on top, x-coordinate coil 8 at the bottom. Row leads X_{1} (16) and X_{2} (18) pass through the x coils of their row in series to X_{1}' and X_{2}'; column leads Y_{1} (20) and Y_{2} (22) run down through the y coils to Y_{1}' and Y_{2}'. The sensing coils of each row are in series between ground (right) and a rectifier (24, 28) feeding output 26. Small semicircular hops are crossings without connection.
figs.3: The eight cores of a 2 x 2 x 2 array, drawn at the corners of a box in perspective, each threaded straight through by one X, one Y and one Z wire (wires drawn as double lines). Each lead runs from its unprimed to its primed end through the four cores of one plane: X_{1} the upper layer, X_{2} the lower, the Y and Z leads the two vertical planes in each direction. A core is chosen by the one X, Y and Z plane that all pass through it.
figs.4: A 4 x 4 x 4 block of 64 cores, each small cube standing for one core; most leads are omitted. Each three-digit number on the front face gives the core's x, y and z lead numbers: X_{1}-X_{4} (left) are the horizontal layers, Z_{1}-Z_{4} (bottom) the vertical slices from right to left, and Y_{1}-Y_{4} (right side) the vertical planes from front to back, so the front face is the Y_{1} plane. S at the upper left is the output line, fed through rectifiers (diode symbols) on the top face; S_{1} at lower left is the grounded end of the sensing circuit.
figs.4a: One core of the array: three exciting wires X_{1}-X_{1}', Y_{1}-Y_{1}' and Z_{1}-Z_{1}' and a sense wire S, its other end grounded, each drawn as a small winding on the ring.
figs.5: Charge-voltage loop of an ideal ferroelectric, the counterpart of Fig. 1. +Q_{R} and -Q_{R} are the remanent charges that store 1 and 0, and ±V_{c} the coercive voltages. A half drive V_{m}/2 stays inside V_{c} and leaves the state unchanged; the full V_{m} reverses it.
figs.6: Four ferroelectric capacitors (slabs) S_{11}-S_{22} in a two-coordinate array. One plate of each slab goes to its row terminal X_{1} or X_{2}; the other goes to its column terminal Y_{1} or Y_{2} through sensing resistor 51 or 55. An X terminal and a Y terminal driven at opposite half voltages put the full V_{m} across only the slab where they cross. The isolating devices (ISO) across each resistor feed mixer M, which gives the output; the hop on the left column wire is a crossing of X_{1}.
figs.7: One three-coordinate storage unit. The X and Y terminals reach one plate (the XY plate) through the nearly equal resistors R_{x} and R_{y}, which act as a voltage divider; Z connects directly to the other plate. The printed voltages are the values each terminal can be switched to. The XY plate is at ±V_{m}/2 when one of X or Y is at ±V_{m} and the other is at 0, and at 0 when they are at opposite polarities; with Z at the opposite half voltage the slab then sees the full V_{m}.
figs.8: The eight-core wiring of Fig. 3 laid out flat. Cores 1-8 are drawn as rectangular rings, each lead entering on the left and leaving at its primed end on the right. Each lead threads four of the eight cores in a staggered pattern: X_{1} cores 1-4 and X_{2} cores 5-8; Y_{1} cores 1, 2, 5, 6 and Y_{2} cores 3, 4, 7, 8; Z_{1} the odd and Z_{2} the even cores. Every core thus gets a different X, Y, Z combination. The text notes this layout works for any number of coordinates.
figs.9: Eight ferroelectric units of the Fig. 7 type, numbered 1-8, wired in the same pattern as the cores of Fig. 8. In each unit the vertical resistor goes to a Y line and the horizontal resistor to an X line, and the capacitor's other plate goes to Z_{1} (odd units) or Z_{2} (even units). The resistors in the Z_{1} and Z_{2} lines at the lower left are the sensing resistors, read through the isolating devices (ISO) and mixer M. Dots are junctions; hops are crossings.

parts.6: In Fig. 2 the cores; in Figs. 8 and 9 the numerals 1-8 instead number the eight cores or storage units, so 6 there is the sixth one.
parts.8: In Fig. 2 the x-coordinate coil; in Figs. 8 and 9 the numeral 8 marks the eighth core or storage unit.
parts.111: Core numbers give the x, y and z lead through the core, in that order: 111 is the core on X_{1}, Y_{1} and Z_{1}.
parts.212: Core on leads X_{2}, Y_{1} and Z_{2}, numbered on the drawing but not discussed individually in the text.
parts.S: Sense wire: in Fig. 4a the single-turn sense winding through the core, in Fig. 4 the output line reached through the rectifiers. The text describes a fourth coil on each core for sensing purposes.
parts.X_{1}': Opposite end of lead X_{1}. The text says the opposite terminal of each lead is switched at the same time, so current can pass in either direction. Same for the other primed leads.
parts.ISO: The text gives an ordinary vacuum tube or transformer as examples.
parts.1: In Figs. 8 and 9 the numerals 1-8 number the eight cores or ferroelectric storage units.

glossary.def: Driving a core with several partial currents, each too weak to switch it alone, so that only the core where all of them meet switches.
A core that receives only some of the coincident drives (H_{1} rather than 2H_{1}, or V_{m}/2 rather than V_{m}); it must stay in its state.
A B-H (or Q-V) loop with flat tops and steep sides, so there is a sharp switching threshold and two stable remanent states.
The magnetization (or charge) left after the drive is removed; points A and D in Fig. 1, +Q_{R} and -Q_{R} in Fig. 5.
The field at which the magnetization reverses; V_{c} is the corresponding voltage for a ferroelectric.
The magnetizing effect of a current in a winding, proportional to current times turns.
Reading by driving the element to a known state, which erases the stored bit; it must be rewritten if it is to be kept.
A winding (here often a single wire) through every core of a group, which picks up the voltage pulse when one of them reverses.
Later name for an opposing current that keeps half-selected cores from switching; here, the -H_{1} current on the unselected Z leads.
A dielectric whose electric polarization stays after the field is removed and can be reversed by a large enough field.
Here a diode, passing current in one direction only.
A switching circuit that routes a drive pulse to one of many leads, used to select the coordinate leads.
A computer that handles all bits of a word at once; one core array per bit, all addressed together.
